problemStatement.formal: \text{Represent the shape of incompleteness arguments using an abstract Formula type and a placeholder Provable predicate.}
problemStatement.plain: A pedagogical Lean scaffold for the structure of Godel's first and second incompleteness theorems, Lob's theorem, and Rosser-style undecidability.
whyMatters: Makes the self-reference and provability-predicate architecture visible in a small Lean file
Shows which pieces would need real syntax, proof checking, and representability machinery in a full formalization
Keeps the record honest that the file is explanatory rather than a substantive mechanized Godel proof

proven: Formula, Provable, Consistent, Complete, G, Con, LobSentence, and RosserSentence scaffolding
first_incompleteness, second_incompleteness, lobs_theorem, and rosser_undecidable as structural theorems over the placeholder model
0 direct axioms and 0 code sorries in the scaffold
open: A real Godel formalization would require formal syntax, Godel numbering, proof verification, primitive recursive functions, and representability theorems
knownResults.goal: Document the completed pedagogical scaffold without claiming a full incompleteness formalization

currentState.focus: Pedagogical scaffold complete: 437 lines, 10 public theorem/lemma declarations, 12 defs, 0 direct axioms, and 0 sorries.

knowledge.progressSummary: COMPLETED: GodelIncompleteness.lean is a 437-line explanatory scaffold with 10 public theorem/lemma declarations, 12 defs, 0 direct axioms, and 0 sorries. Provable is intentionally defined as false, so the file illustrates proof architecture rather than proving incompleteness for a real formal system.
insights: The file is intentionally pedagogical: Provable is defined as false, so theorem statements are vacuous under the model.
A substantive mechanization would need thousands of lines of syntax, encoding, proof verification, and representability infrastructure.
The scaffold is still useful as a compact map of the dependencies between diagonalization, consistency, provability, and self-reference.
